content_voiceover: This slide addresses a common exam trap, the assumption that a negative family history rules out hemophilia. In reality, hemophilia is usually inherited in an X-linked pattern, but sporadic, meaning de novo, cases are quite common, especially in severe disease. For hemophilia A, about fifty-five percent of severe cases arise from new mutations with no family history, while sporadic cases make up about thirty percent of mild to moderate disease. For hemophilia B, the sporadic rate is somewhat lower but still substantial, about forty percent of severe cases and about thirty percent of mild to moderate cases occur without a family history. The clinical takeaway is that you cannot exclude a hemophilia diagnosis just because a patient has no relatives with a bleeding disorder. Especially in a male infant or child presenting with unexplained bruising or bleeding, a new spontaneous mutation is a very plausible explanation, and testing should proceed regardless of family history.
keypoints: Family history absence does not rule out hemophilia
About 55% of severe hemophilia A cases are sporadic, new mutations
About 40% of severe hemophilia B cases are sporadic
Roughly 30% of mild-to-moderate cases in both types are sporadic
keypoint_voiceover: The single most important takeaway is that a negative family history never excludes hemophilia. Sporadic, new mutations account for over half of severe hemophilia A cases and around forty percent of severe hemophilia B cases. Keep this in mind whenever you evaluate an unexplained bleeding presentation in a child.
